title: How much of the trading environment belongs in a backtest?
author: NoTart7529
selftext:
I've been thinking about how easy it is to make a backtest look comprehensive while still leaving out some of the things that can affect the strategy once it's actually running.  

Entries, exits, spreads, slippage and drawdown are the obvious ones. Account-level constraints can be harder to reproduce. A daily loss limit, maximum loss threshold or restriction on how positions can be managed can change the behaviour of a system even if the underlying strategy hasn't changed. Prop accounts make this pretty interesting because the trading environment comes with another layer of rules. I've seen this with aifo 1step and 2 step challenges where EAs are permitted but automated trading still has to operate within the firm's other trading conditions.  A strategy can pass every historical test and still run into problems once those account conditions are added. 

Testing the strategy and testing its ability to operate within the account are really two different exercises. How much of the trading environment do you try to reproduce when testing an automated strategy?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
most of the environment, because the account rules are where my stuff died, not the signal. my backtester only grades what the strategy itself can see: options filled on whichever side of the quote you'd actually get, the bar open for stocks, no look-ahead. a daily loss stop or a max position count I run as a second pass over the trade list, because once you bake the prop rules into the strategy you can't tell which of the two failed.

the split you describe is how I'd do it too. test the rule, then replay its trades through the account rules and count the days it would have been locked out. that second number is usually the surprise.

Quantradin, the backtester I built, does the first pass and runs survivors as paper bots. quantradin.com, everything on it is paper. the account-rules layer is still a spreadsheet for me.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I'd treat them as two separate tests. First the strategy on its own with realistic costs, then the same trades run through a simulator of the account rules (daily loss limit, max drawdown measured on equity including open P&L, minimum trading days, news restrictions, lot limits), so you see the pass rate and not just the profit. Bootstrapping the trade order (in blocks) shows how often a bad sequence breaches a limit even when the average is fine. Many prop firms also restrict trading around scheduled releases, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for building that rule into the test.
